narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles were deeply rooted in their cultural heritage and identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of afro-textured hair, was likely a common style during this time period, as it has been a staple in African cultures for centuries. Cornrows, another traditional African braiding practice, may have also been popular among women seeking to preserve and celebrate their natural hair texture. Unfortunately, the source material does not provide specific information about hairstyles and hair culture during the 1950s, but based on the existing text, it is possible that protective styles like Bantu knots or box braids were used by women to minimize hair manipulation and breakage. The Jheri curl, a popular hairstyle among Black Americans in later decades, has no mention in the source material for this era, suggesting its emergence may have occurred after the 1950s.
